{{Short description|Mathematical sequence}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Leray spectral sequence''' was a pioneering example in [[homological algebra]], introduced in 1946<ref name="LerHomRep">{{Cite journal|title = L'anneau d'homologie d'une représentation|journal = [[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences]] |pages = 1366–1368|volume = 222 |year=1946|first = Jean|last = Leray|authorlink=Jean Leray|url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k31740/f1366.item#}}</ref><ref name="LerOflag">{{Cite journal|title = Leray in Oflag XVIIA : the origins of sheaf theory, sheaf cohomology, and spectral sequences, Jean Leray (1906–1998)|url = http://www-math.mit.edu/~hrm/papers/ss.pdf|journal = Gaz. Math.|pages = 17–34|volume = 84|year= 2000|first = Haynes|last = Miller|authorlink=Haynes Miller}}</ref> by [[Jean Leray]]. It is usually seen nowadays as a special case of the [[Grothendieck spectral sequence]].

==Definition==
Let <math>f:X\to Y</math> be a continuous map of topological spaces, which in particular gives a [[functor]] <math>f_*</math> from [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves of abelian groups]] on <math>X</math> to sheaves of abelian groups on <math>Y</math>. Composing this with the functor <math>\Gamma</math> of taking sections on <math>\text{Sh}_\text{Ab}(Y)</math> is the same as taking sections on <math>\text{Sh}_\text{Ab}(X)</math>, by the definition of the direct image functor <math>f_*</math>:

:<math>\mathrm{Sh_{Ab}} (X) \xrightarrow{f_*} \mathrm{Sh_{Ab}}(Y) \xrightarrow{\Gamma} \mathrm{Ab}.</math>

Thus the [[Derived functor|derived functors]] of <math>\Gamma \circ f_*</math> compute the [[sheaf cohomology]] for <math>X</math>:

:<math> R^i (\Gamma \cdot f_*)(\mathcal{F})=H^i(X,\mathcal{F}).</math>

But because <math>f_*</math> and <math>\Gamma</math> send [[Injective object|injective objects]] in <math>\text{Sh}_\text{Ab}(X)</math> to <math>\Gamma</math>-[[Acyclic object|acyclic objects]] in <math>\text{Sh}_\text{Ab}(Y)</math>, there is a [[spectral sequence]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Dimca|first= Alexandru|authorlink=Alexandru Dimca|title=Sheaves in Topology|series= Universitext|date=2004|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|location= Berlin, Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-642-18868-8|oclc=851731478|doi=
10.1007/978-3-642-18868-8}}</ref><sup>pg 33,19</sup> whose second page is 

:<math> E^{pq}_2=(R^p\Gamma \cdot R^q f_*)(\mathcal{F})=H^p(Y,R^qf_*(\mathcal{F})) ,</math>

and which converges to 

:<math> E^{p+q} = R^{p+q}(\Gamma \circ f_*)(\mathcal{F})= H^{p+q}(X,\mathcal{F}) .</math>

This is called the '''Leray spectral sequence'''. 

=== Generalizing to other sheaves and complexes of sheaves ===
Note this result can be generalized by instead considering sheaves of modules over a [[locally constant sheaf]] of rings <math>\underline{A}</math> for a fixed commutative ring <math>A</math>. Then, the sheaves will be sheaves of <math>\underline{A}</math>-modules, where for an open set <math>U \subset X</math>, such a sheaf <math>\mathcal{F} \in \text{Sh}_{\underline{A}}(X)</math> is an <math>\underline{A}(U)</math>-module for <math>\mathcal{F}(U)</math>. In addition, instead of sheaves, we could consider complexes of sheaves bounded below <math>\mathcal{F}^\bullet \in D^+_{\underline{A}}(X)</math> for the [[derived category]] of <math>\text{Sh}_{\underline{A}}(X)</math>. Then, one replaces sheaf cohomology with [[Hyperhomology|sheaf hypercohomology]].

=== Construction ===
The existence of the Leray spectral sequence is a direct application of the [[Grothendieck spectral sequence]]<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 19</sup>. This states that given additive functors

:<math>\mathcal{A} \xrightarrow{G}\mathcal{B} \xrightarrow{F} \mathcal{C}</math>

between [[Abelian categories]] having [[enough injectives]], <math>F</math> a [[Left exact functor|left-exact functor]], and <math>G</math> sending injective objects to <math>F</math>-acyclic objects, then there is an isomorphism of [[Derived functor|derived functors]]

:<math>R^+(F\circ G) \simeq R^+F\circ R^+G </math>

for the derived categories <math>D^+(\mathcal{A}),D^+(\mathcal{B}), D^+(\mathcal{C})</math>. In the example above, we have the composition of derived functors

:<math>D^+(\text{Sh}_\text{Ab}(X)) \xrightarrow{Rf_*} D^+(\text{Sh}_\text{Ab}(Y)) \xrightarrow{\Gamma} D^+(\text{Ab}).</math>

==Classical definition==

Let <math>f\colon X\to Y</math> be a continuous map of [[smooth manifolds]]. If <math>\mathcal{U} = \{U_i\}_{i \in I}</math> is an open cover of {{nowrap|<math>Y</math>,}} form the [[Čech complex]] of a sheaf <math>\mathcal{F} \in \text{Sh}(X)</math> with respect to cover <math>f^{-1}(U)</math> of {{nowrap|<math>X</math>:}}

:<math> \text{C}^p(f^{-1}\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{F})</math>

The boundary maps <math>d^p\colon C^p \to C^{p+1}</math> and maps <math>\delta^q\colon \Omega^q_X \to \Omega_X^{q+1}</math> of sheaves on <math>X</math> together give a boundary map on the double complex <math> \text{C}^p(f^{-1}\mathcal{U}, \Omega_X^q)</math>

:<math> D=d+\delta \colon   C^\bullet(f^{-1}\mathcal{U},\Omega_X^\bullet)\longrightarrow C^\bullet(f^{-1}\mathcal{U},\Omega_X^\bullet) .</math>

This [[double complex]] is also a single complex graded by {{nowrap|<math>n=p+q</math>,}} with respect to which <math>D</math> is a boundary map. If each finite intersection of the <math>U_i</math> is [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphic]] to {{nowrap|<math>\R^n</math>,}} one can show that the cohomology 

:<math>H_D^n( C^\bullet(f^{-1}\mathcal{U},\Omega_X^\bullet)) = H_\text{dR}^n(X,\R)</math>

of this complex is the [[de Rham cohomology]] of {{nowrap|<math>X</math>.}}<ref name="Bott-Tu">{{Cite book|last1=Bott|first1= Raoul| author1-link=Raoul Bott|title=Differential forms in algebraic topology|last2=Tu|first2= Loring W.|series=[[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]|date= 1982|volume=82|
isbn=978-0-387-90613-3|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|location=New York-Berlin|oclc=7597142|doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-3951-0}}</ref>{{rp|96}}<!--Proposition 8.8--> Moreover,<ref name="Bott-Tu"/>{{rp|179}}<!--Leray's construction--><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Griffiths| first1=Phillip|author1-link=Phillip Griffiths|title=Principles of algebraic geometry|year=1978|publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]]|last2=Harris|first2= Joe|author2-link=Joe Harris (mathematician)| isbn=0-471-32792-1|location=New York|oclc=3843444|page=443}}</ref><!--the statement in italics--> 
any double complex has a spectral sequence ''E'' with

:<math> E_\infty^{n-p,p} = \text{the }p\text{th graded part of } H^n_{dR}( C^\bullet(f^{-1}\mathcal{U},\Omega_X^\bullet))</math>

(so that the sum of these is {{nowrap|<math>H^n_{dR}</math>),}} and 

:<math> E_2^{p,q} = H^p(f^{-1}\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{H}^q),</math>

where <math> \mathcal{H}^q</math> is the presheaf on ''Y'' sending {{nowrap|<math>U \mapsto H^q(f^{-1}(U), F) </math>.}} In this context, this is called the Leray spectral sequence.

The modern definition subsumes this, because the higher direct image functor <math>R^pf_*(F)</math> is the sheafification of the presheaf {{nowrap|<math>U \mapsto H^q(f^{-1}(U), F)</math>.}}

==Examples==

* Let <math>X,F</math> be [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifolds]], and <math>X</math> be [[Simply connected space|simply connected]], so <math>\pi_1(X) = 0</math>. We calculate the Leray spectral sequence of the projection <math>f\colon X\times F \to X</math>. If the cover <math>\mathcal{U} = \{U_i\}_{i \in I}</math> is good (finite intersections are <math>\R^n</math>) then

::<math> \mathcal{H}^p(f^{-1}U_i)\simeq H^q(F)</math>
:Since <math>X</math> is simply connected, any locally constant presheaf is constant, so this is the constant presheaf <math>H^q(F) = \underline{\R}^{n_q}</math>. So the second page of the Leray spectral sequence is
::<math> E_2^{p,q} = H^p(f^{-1}\mathcal{U}, H^q(F))=H^p(f^{-1}\mathcal{U}, \R)\otimes H^q(F)</math>
:As the cover <math>\{f^{-1}(U_i)\}_{i \in I}</math> of <math>X\times F</math> is also good, <math>H^p(f^{-1}(U_i);\R) \cong H^p(f;\R)</math>. So
::<math> E_2^{p,q} = H^p(X)\otimes H^q(F) \ \Longrightarrow \  H^{p+q}(X\times F,\R)</math>
: Here is the first place we use that <math>f</math> is a projection and not just a fibre bundle: every element of <math>E_2</math> is an actual closed [[differential form]] on all of <math>X\times F</math>, so applying both ''d'' and <math>\delta</math> to them gives zero. Thus <math>E_\infty = E_2</math>. This proves the [[Künneth theorem]] for <math>X</math> simply connected:
::<math> H^\bullet(X\times Y,\R)\simeq H^\bullet(X)\otimes H^\bullet(Y)</math>

* If <math>f\colon X \to Y</math> is a general [[fiber bundle]] with fibre <math>F</math>, the above applies, except that <math>V^p \to H^p(f^{-1}V,H^q)</math> is only a locally constant presheaf, not constant.

* All example computations with the [[Serre spectral sequence]] are the Leray sequence for the constant sheaf.

== Degeneration theorem ==
In the category of [[Quasi-projective variety|quasi-projective varieties]] over <math>\Complex</math>, there is a degeneration theorem proved by [[Pierre Deligne]] and Blanchard for the Leray spectral sequence, which states that a smooth projective morphism of varieties <math>f\colon X \to Y</math> gives us that the <math>E_2</math>-page of the spectral sequence for <math>\underline{\Q}_X</math> degenerates, hence
:<math>
H^k(X;\Q) \cong \bigoplus_{p + q = k} H^{p}(Y;\mathbf{R}^qf_*(\underline{\Q}_X)).
</math>
Easy examples can be computed if {{mvar|Y}} is simply connected; for example a complete intersection of dimension <math>\geq 2</math> (this is because of the [[Hurewicz theorem|Hurewicz homomorphism]] and the [[Lefschetz hyperplane theorem]]). In this case the local systems <math>\mathbf{R}^qf_*(\underline{\Q}_X)</math> will have trivial monodromy, hence <math>\mathbf{R}^qf_*(\underline{\Q}_X) \cong \underline{\Q}_Y^{\oplus l_q}</math>. For example, consider a smooth family <math>f\colon X\to Y</math> of genus 3 curves over a smooth [[K3 surface]]. Then, we have that
:<math>
\begin{align}
\mathbf{R}^0f_*(\underline{\Q}_X) &\cong \underline{\Q}_Y \\
\mathbf{R}^1f_*(\underline{\Q}_X) &\cong \underline{\Q}_Y^{\oplus 6} \\
\mathbf{R}^2f_*(\underline{\Q}_X) &\cong \underline{\Q}_Y
\end{align}
</math>
giving us the <math>E_2</math>-page
:<math>
E_2 = E_\infty = \begin{bmatrix}
H^0(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y) & 0 & H^2(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y) & 0 & H^4(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y) \\
H^0(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y^{\oplus 6}) & 0 & H^2(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y^{\oplus 6}) & 0 & H^4(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y^{\oplus 6}) \\
H^0(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y) & 0 & H^2(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y) & 0 & H^4(Y;\underline{\Q}_Y)
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

=== Example with monodromy ===
Another important example of a smooth projective family is the family associated to the elliptic curves
:<math>
y^2 = x(x-1)(x-t)
</math>
over <math>\mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0, 1, \infty \}</math>. Here the monodromy around {{val|0}} and {{val|1}} can be computed using [[Picard–Lefschetz theory]], giving the monodromy around <math>\infty</math> by composing local monodromies.

==History and connection to other spectral sequences==
At the time of Leray's work, neither of the two concepts involved (spectral sequence, sheaf cohomology) had reached anything like a definitive state. Therefore it is rarely the case that Leray's result is quoted in its original form. After much work, in the seminar of [[Henri Cartan]] in particular, the modern statement was obtained, though not the general Grothendieck spectral sequence.

Earlier (1948/9) the implications for [[fiber bundle]]s were extracted in a form formally identical to that of the [[Serre spectral sequence]], which makes no use of sheaves. This treatment, however, applied to [[Alexander–Spanier cohomology]] with [[Support (mathematics)|compact supports]], as applied to [[proper map]]s of locally compact Hausdorff spaces, as the derivation of the spectral sequence required a [[fine sheaf]] of real [[differential graded algebra]]s on the total space, which was obtained by pulling back the [[de Rham complex]] along an embedding into a sphere. [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], who needed a spectral sequence in ''homology'' that applied to [[path space fibration]]s, whose total spaces are almost never locally compact, thus was unable to use the original Leray spectral sequence and so derived a related spectral sequence whose cohomological variant agrees, for a compact fiber bundle on a well-behaved space with the sequence above.

In the formulation achieved by [[Alexander Grothendieck]] by about 1957, the Leray spectral sequence is the [[Grothendieck spectral sequence]] for the composition of two [[derived functor]]s.
